entry.dc:title: Reclamation of deep mine refuse banks with municipal sewage sludge
entry.dc:creator: Seaker E.M.
entry.dc:description: Municipal sludge was applied on a deep mine anthracite refuse bank at rates of 80 and 108 dry Mg/ha to facilitate vegetation establishment. A monitoring system was installed to determine the effects of the sludge applications on the quality and growth of the vegetative cover, chemical properties of the soil, and chemical and bacteriological quality of the groundwater. Data collected over a 5-year period indicate that the addition of sludge improved the physical and chemical condition of the black, highly acidic refuse material and promoted establishment and continued growth of a complete vegetative cover. Sludge applications resulted in slight increases in some trace metal concentrations in the surface soil and in the vegetation. However, soil concentrations were within the normal range found in U.S. soils. Vegetation foliar trace metal concentrations were well below plant tolerance levels and no phytotoxicity symptoms were ever observed. In general, the sludge applications had no significant adverse effect on the chemical or bacteriological quality of groundwater. The results indicate that single applications of stabilized municipal sludge, applied at rates up to 108 dry Mg/ha with lime, can be used in an environmentally safe manner to revegetate coal refuse banks in the Appalachian mining region, with a cover that is self-maintaining for the 5-year period mandated under the federal Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. © 1983.

entry.dc:title: ACCOMMODATING THE LAND USE PLANNING PROVISIONS OF THE SURFACE MINING CONTROL AND RECLAMATION ACT.
entry.dc:creator: Saperstein L.
entry.dc:description: Approval of surface coal mine permits in the US became more complex with the imposition of certain additional and relatively untested requirements of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (Public Law 95-87). Because of delays built into the schedule for applying this law, the American mining system has not yet seen the full extent of these complexities. Its reclamation and designation sections require recognition of local land use plans. Accommodation to these requirements affords an opportunity to create better links among local land use planners, the state's permitting authority and designation office, and mine designers.

entry.dc:title: An attempt to estimate seismic risk in the Belchatow surface mining area ( Poland).
entry.dc:creator: Kijko A.
entry.dc:description: Observations of seismic activity in the Belchatow area from 17 August 1979 to 25 July 1982 were used to estimate the probability of occurrence of stronger shocks with magnitude M<inf>L</inf>= or >2.0. For this a special method was used, permitting evaluation of seismic risk from limited and even incomplete observations. From the comparison of theoretical and observational data it follows that the adopted mathematical model describes correctly the observed seismicity in the Belchatow surface mining area. It was estimated that the maximum expected magnitude in the area should not exceed M<inf>L</inf>=4.8.-Author

entry.dc:title: UPDATE - RECLAIMING MINE LANDS IN ALASKA.
entry.dc:creator: Maneval D.
entry.dc:description: The Surface Mining Act of 1977 required a study by the National Academy of Sciences regarding the mine reclamation requirements of Alaska. The status of mines operating and planned in Alaska is presented. New mines must establish a baseline inventory of plants and animals in the mine site area as well as determine premining air and water quality. A summary of current research dealing with revegetation on surface mined lands, re-establishment of animal populations, and water treatment process is discussed. Included is prediction of the direction of mine reclamation as more mines enter the industry.

entry.dc:title: UPDATE ON THE IMPACT OF THE SURFACE MINING CONTROL AND RECLAMATION ACT OF 1977 ON PROFESSIONAL LAND SURVEYORS.
entry.dc:creator: Palatiello J.M.
entry.dc:description: Section 507(b)(14) of the Surface Mine Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (Public Law 95-87, 30 U. S. C. 1201) conflicts with the laws of nearly every state in that it preempts registered land surveyors from a lead role in the preparation and certification of maps, plans, and cross-sections of land to be affected by surface mining activity. An informal poll of its members in major coal-producing states by the American Congress on Surveying and Mapping revealed that this provision in the Act not only is in conflict with state law, but also jeopardizes public health, welfare, and safety by neglecting attention to the details of boundary monumentation which could lead to serious and costly litigation in years to come. Furthermore, it adversely impacts employment of surveyors and reduces income opportunities for surveying firms.

entry.dc:title: Stream water quality of two small watersheds as affected by surface coal mining
entry.dc:creator: Dick W.A.
entry.dc:description: Two small watersheds in eastcentral Ohio were selected for investigation of stream water quality prior to, during, and after surface coal mining and reclamation. Water quality was monitored by measuring 39 parameters in the stream-water samples collected. Duration curves for the four parameters regulated by the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) showed that most samples collected from the two study watersheds exceeded the 70 mg L** minus **1 regulation level for suspended solids concentration. Approximately 50 and 30% of the water samples collected at one watershed exceeded the regulation level for manganese (Mn), and 20% of the pH values were also below the lower regulation level. Samples collected at similar flow rates at the other watershed showed concentrations of parameters were either not significantly affected or decreased in the post-reclamation samples, compared with the premine samples.

entry.dc:title: DEVELOPMENTS IN OFF-HIGHWAY TRUCKS.
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.K.
entry.dc:description: Much of the material transportation in surface mining is by trucks consuming about 50% of the total operating costs. Developments in equipment technology to reduce costs include trolley power assist, automatic truck control systems, mechanical drive trucks in the 85-120t range and hydraulic shovels.

entry.dc:creator: West R.
entry.dc:description: Rail haulage, although normally not a favored alternative for surface operations, may still be viable in new mines under specific conditions. The author reviews rail haulage trends in the United States.

entry.dc:title: REDUCE HIGHWALLS - AND COSTS, TOO.
entry.dc:creator: Chironis N.
entry.dc:description: One of the principal goals of the Federal Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (Public Law 95-87) is the elimination of all highwalls and the return of coal-mined lands to approximate original contour. By setting up graphical curves for dozer and blasting costs, the most economical contour for backfilling highwalls can be selected.

entry.dc:title: UNDERGROUND COAL WASTE DISPOSAL: CAN IT BE COST EFFECTIVE?
entry.dc:creator: Gaffney D.
entry.dc:description: While it does not require underground disposal of coal wastes, the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) has called attention to this alternative and is mandated by Public Law 95-87 to promote research for its development. Recent research has defined several underground disposal options applicable to active mines and identified the need to critically evaluate site-specific economics.

entry.dc:title: Consol's slurry system.
entry.dc:creator: Douglas Dahl H.
entry.prism:publicationName: In Coal Technology 83 6th Int Coal Lignite Utilization Exhib Conf Houston U S A Nov 15 17 1983
entry.dc:description: Nearly 15 years of research, development, and in mine operation to provide a unique technology for continuous haulage of run of mine, coarse coal from underground production zones to its destination outside the mine and even beyond. The Loveridge project is a full scale demonstration of the technology as applied to underground mining. Commercialization is the culmination of these development efforts and is occurring in coal mining. Extension of the technology into surface mining, coal delivery to users, tunnelling, and other fields is considered feasible. (from authors' abstract)

entry.dc:title: ROLE OF LOADING AND HAULING EQUIPMENT IN SURFACE MINING.
entry.dc:creator: Singhal R.
entry.dc:description: This paper reviews some of the equipment and systems used on a major scale for loading and transportation in surface mining of coal. As a general trend conveyors and conveyor related systems are finding greater acceptance due to their lower operation costs given the present day fuel costs. Mobile equipment has found new applications as they require lower initial capital investments. Hydraulic shovels and hydraulic bucket wheel excavators dicharging directly either into trucks or hoppers discharging on to various types of conveyor systems are finding increasing application. The 1980s will see further development of large size truck, automatic truck control and automatic dispatch systems.

entry.dc:title: Automatic lubrication systems favored.
entry.dc:creator: Happ J.
entry.dc:description: Automated centralized lubrication systems suitable for mobile surface mining equipment were compared and contrasted for various applications. Closer control of machine lubrication was achieved. The quantity and type of lubricant, lubricating points and lubricating frequency were determined in advance and could be optimised by subsequent adjustments. Machine productivity was improved and lubricant costs were minimised. (H.C.B.)

entry.dc:title: Some aspects of mining subsidence and its control in the US coalfields
entry.dc:creator: Karmis N.
entry.dc:description: The problem of surface subsidence is rapidly becoming an important environmental consideration of active as well as abandoned mining operations in the USA. The damages attributed to this phenomenon range from simple land settlement to severe structural damage and have been experienced in both rural and urban areas spreading across thirty states. This paper presents a discussion on mining subsidence and its characteristics above US longwall and room-and-pillar mines. The influence of the geological controls on subsidence is discussed in detail and the effects of subsidence on man and his environment are presented and exemplified. In addition, a historical review of rules and regulations governing subsidence-related problems is given, leading to Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, and finally, the new regulations being developed under the regulatory reform program are discussed. © 1982 Science and technology letters.

entry.dc:title: Engineering's role in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Schivley W.W.
entry.prism:publicationName: Journal of the Energy Division Proceedings of the ASCE
entry.dc:description: As a result of Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, many new consulting opportunities are being developed by engineering firms. Many of these opportunities are in the form of established services given a new perspective to meet regulatory compliance and/or reclamation data base requirements. Some of these engineering and environmental services are discussed and, utilizing actual case study experience, a scenario is presented of the engineering firm's new role in this most controversial legislation. Given the environmental ethics established in the 1970's, it seems unlikely that our nation's environmental protection will be rescinded. With this future course of action the engineering firm should continue to play a major role in the environmental aspects of surface mining.

entry.dc:title: Changes in the groundwater due to surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Libicki J.
entry.dc:description: Open-cast mining operations conducted below groundwater table often affect the drawdown of the water table over large areas which as a consequence changes the natural regional hydrological balance. Remedial measures may include construction of new water intakes, and changes in the land usage may be necessary. Tipping of wastes (most often coal wastes and ashes) affects ground water pollution. Instead of removal of effects, preventive methods are recommended. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

entry.dc:title: Control of groundwater in surface mining
entry.dc:creator: Brawner C.O.
entry.dc:description: The presence of groundwater in surface mining operations often creates serious problems. The most important is generally a reduction in stability of the pit slopes. This is caused by pore water pressures and hydrodynamic shock due to blasting which reduce the shear strength and seepage pressures, water in tension cracks and increased unit weight which increase the shear stress. Groundwater and seepage also increase the cost of pit drainage, shipping, drilling and blasting, tyre wear and equipment maintenance. Surface erosion may also be increased and, in northern climates, ice flows on the slopes may occur. Procedures have been developed in the field of soil mechanics and engineering of dams to obtain quantitative data on pore water pressures and rock permeability, to evaluate the influence of pore water and seepage pressures on stability and to estimate the magnitude of ground-water flow. Based on field investigations, a design can be prepared for the control of groundwater in the slope and in the pit. Methods of control include the use of horizontal drains, blasted toe drains, construction of adits or drainage tunnels and pumping from wells in or outside of the pit. Recent research indicates that subsurface drainage can be augmented by applying a vacuum or by selective blasting. Instrumentation should be installed to monitor the groundwater changes created by drainage. Typical case histories are described that indicate the approach used to evaluate groundwater conditions. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

entry.dc:title: Groundwater problems in surface coal mining in Scotland
entry.dc:creator: Norton P.J.
entry.dc:description: The paper reviews the problems encountered with groundwater in surface mining in Scotland. The problems which occur at various stages of the mining process from initial exploration to mine planning and final restoration are referred to. Special consideration is given to mine drainage and pumping methods. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.
